questions.question: When is a strategy profile $\sigma^*$ of an extensive-form game $\Gamma$ a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE)?
options: When, for every subgame $\Gamma'$ of $\Gamma$, the restriction of $\sigma^*$ to $\Gamma'$ is a Nash equilibrium of $\Gamma'$.
When $\sigma^*$ is a Nash equilibrium of $\Gamma$ and every subgame of $\Gamma$ is reached with positive probability.
When, for every subgame reached under $\sigma^*$, the restriction of $\sigma^*$ is a Nash equilibrium of that subgame.
When the restriction of $\sigma^*$ to the last subgame on the path of play is a Nash equilibrium of that subgame.

questions.question: Why is every subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium of an extensive-form game $\Gamma$ also a Nash equilibrium of $\Gamma$?
options: Because Nash equilibria are defined as profiles that are optimal in every subgame of the game.
Because $\Gamma$ is a subgame of itself, so the restriction to $\Gamma$, the whole profile, is a Nash equilibrium.
Because every game has a unique Nash equilibrium, which subgame perfection must select.
Because subgame perfection only checks subgames on the path, and Nash equilibrium checks the same.

questions.question: Player 1 takes Out, with payoffs $(2,2)$, or In; then player 1 picks $A$ or $B$ while player 2 simultaneously picks $a$ or $b$: $(A,a)\mapsto(3,1)$, $(B,b)\mapsto(1,3)$, and $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. A student reports an SPNE as "player 1 takes Out, so the outcome is $(2,2)$". Why is this not a complete answer?
options: It omits nothing; as In is never played, plans after In are not part of an SPNE.
It omits only player 2's action; player 1's choice of Out is a complete strategy.
It omits the payoffs of the subgame, which define the equilibrium together with Out.
It omits the plans after In; both (Out $B$, $b$) and Out with the mixed plan give $(2,2)$.

questions.question: An extensive-form game $\Gamma$ has no subgame other than $\Gamma$ itself. How are its subgame-perfect Nash equilibria related to its Nash equilibria?
options: There are none, since there is no subgame to test the profile in.
They are the Nash equilibria that are also in pure strategies.
They coincide: the only condition is Nash equilibrium in $\Gamma$.
They are the Nash equilibria that give every player the most.

questions.question: In the entry game, the entrant chooses Out, giving $(0,2)$ to (entrant, incumbent), or In; after In the incumbent chooses Accommodate ($A$), $(1,1)$, or Fight ($F$), $(-1,-1)$. Which profile is the unique subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium?
options: (Out, $F$)
(Out, $A$)

questions.question: In an entry game, Out gives $(0,2)$ to (entrant, incumbent). After In, Accommodate gives $(1,1)$ and Fight gives $(-1,2)$. Which profile is the subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium?
options: (In, Accommodate)
(Out, Fight)
(In, Fight)
(Out, Accommodate)

questions.question: The simultaneous Battle of the Sexes, with $(O,O)\mapsto(2,1)$, $(F,F)\mapsto(1,2)$ and $(0,0)$ after a mismatch, is drawn as a tree in which player 2 does not observe player 1's move. How many pure-strategy subgame-perfect Nash equilibria does it have?

Player 1 takes Out, with payoffs $(2,2)$, or In; then player 1 picks $A$ or $B$ while player 2 simultaneously picks $a$ or $b$: $(A,a)\mapsto(3,1)$, $(B,b)\mapsto(1,3)$, and $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. Why does this game have three different subgame-perfect Nash equilibria?
options: The subgame after In has three Nash equilibria, and each leads to its own SPNE.
Player 1 can choose Out or In, and each choice defines its own SPNE.
Player 2 has two strategies and player 1 has a third option, Out.
Two of the three are Nash equilibria that are not subgame perfect.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses Out, giving $(1,-1)$, or In; after In both play Matching Pennies simultaneously (player 1 gets $1$ on a match and $-1$ otherwise; player 2 the opposite). Does this game have a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium in pure strategies?
options: Yes: player 1 takes Out, so the subgame never matters for subgame perfection.
No: games with a simultaneous subgame never have a subgame-perfect equilibrium.
No: the subgame has only a mixed equilibrium, so any SPNE must mix after In.
Yes: every finite extensive-form game has a pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium.

questions.question: Player 1 takes Out, with payoffs $(2,2)$, or In; then player 1 picks $A$ or $B$ while player 2 simultaneously picks $a$ or $b$: $(A,a)\mapsto(3,1)$, $(B,b)\mapsto(1,3)$, and $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. In the subgame's mixed equilibrium (player 1: $A$ w.p. $\tfrac{3}{4}$; player 2: $a$ w.p. $\tfrac{1}{4}$), player 1 expects $\tfrac{3}{4}$. In the SPNE built on it, what does player 1 do at the root?
options: In, since the subgame is mixed.
In with probability $\tfrac{3}{4}$.
Out, since $\tfrac{3}{4}<2$.
Out with probability $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses Stop, $(1,0)$, or Continue; player 2 then chooses Stop, $(0,2)$, or Continue; player 1 then chooses Stop, $(3,1)$, or Continue, $(2,4)$. All moves are observed. Which profile is the subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium?
options: Player 1: Stop; player 2: Stop.
Player 1: (Stop, Stop); player 2: Stop.
Player 1: (Continue, Continue); player 2: Continue.
Player 1: (Stop, Continue); player 2: Stop.

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $O$ or $F$; player 2 observes it and chooses $O$ or $F$; payoffs $(O,O)\mapsto(2,1)$, $(F,F)\mapsto(1,2)$, $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. Player 2's strategies are written (reply to $O$, reply to $F$). Its pure Nash equilibria are $(O, OO)$, $(O, OF)$ and $(F, FF)$. Which of them is subgame perfect?
options: Only $(O, OF)$.
Only $(F, FF)$.
Only $(O, OO)$.
All three.

questions.question: Player 1 makes a move that player 2 cannot observe, and player 2 then moves at a single information set containing both of her nodes. Why may subgame perfection fail to remove an implausible Nash equilibrium in such a game?
options: Subgame perfection never applies to games in which some move is not observed by the other player.
Player 2's information set starts its own subgame, in which every action is a Nash equilibrium.
The game may have no subgame other than itself, so every Nash equilibrium is subgame perfect.
Implausible behaviour is removed only in mixed strategies, which subgame perfection does not consider.

questions.question: Player 1 takes Out, with payoffs $(2,2)$, or In; then player 1 picks $A$ or $B$ while player 2 simultaneously picks $a$ or $b$: $(A,a)\mapsto(3,1)$, $(B,b)\mapsto(1,3)$, and $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. Consider the profile in which player 1 takes Out and plans $A$ after In, and player 2 plays $b$. Which statement about this profile is correct?
options: It is an SPNE, because Out is optimal for player 1 given player 2's strategy $b$.
It is a Nash equilibrium but not an SPNE: $(A,b)$ is not an equilibrium of the subgame.
It is not a Nash equilibrium, because player 1 could switch to In with $A$ and get $3$.
It is an SPNE, because the subgame after In is never reached under this profile.

questions.question: Player 1 takes Out, with payoffs $(\tfrac{1}{2},2)$, or In; then both choose simultaneously: $(A,a)\mapsto(3,1)$, $(B,b)\mapsto(1,3)$, $(0,0)$ after a mismatch. The subgame has the equilibria $(A,a)$, $(B,b)$ and a mixed one worth $\tfrac{3}{4}$ to player 1. How many SPNE have player 1 choose In?
options: Only $1$
Only $2$
All $3$
None

questions.question: Subgame perfection refines Nash equilibrium in extensive-form games. What kind of behaviour does it rule out that Nash equilibrium allows?
options: Behaviour that gives some player a payoff lower than she would get in another Nash equilibrium.
Non-equilibrium play in unreached subgames, such as a threat that would not be carried out.
Any use of mixed strategies, since subgame perfection requires every player to use pure strategies.
Behaviour on the path of play that is not a best response to the other players' strategies.

questions.question: Consider a finite extensive-form game of perfect information without moves of Nature, in which no player has the same payoff at two different terminal nodes. How many pure-strategy subgame-perfect Nash equilibria does it have?
options: At least two.
Possibly none.
One per player.
Exactly one.

questions.question: In a finite game of perfect information without moves of Nature, the condition "no player has the same payoff at two different terminal nodes" guarantees a unique pure SPNE. Must such a game in which some player does have equal payoffs at two terminal nodes have several pure SPNE?
options: Yes: any pair of equal payoffs creates a tie in the backward induction, and every tie produces a second pure SPNE.
Yes: without the condition a pure SPNE need not even exist, let alone be unique.
No: equal payoffs at terminal nodes never affect the number of pure SPNE in a game of perfect information.
No: the condition is sufficient, not necessary; only indifference at a mover's own node creates extra pure SPNE.
